variants.candidate: Old texts have it that metal keeps to the stone and is born where the ground stays damp. Ore does not form in the open. It waits under the hill, pressed by rock and fed by slow water, for longer than anything struck from it lasts. Earth gives the blade its substance first and its patience second, and a blade that forgets the ground it came from loses the second gift first.
variants.original: Metal is born of earth, the old texts say: it lies in the mountain, gathered in stone, grown by slow pressure and the moisture of deep ground. Nothing hurries it. The mountain holds the ore for ages before any edge is struck from it, and every blade remembers the patience of the rock that made it.

variants.candidate: The hard overcomes the soft, the old texts say, so metal overcomes wood. A blade is only a blade against something that resists it: timber gives the edge its reason, and the grain decides whether a stroke runs clean. Wood never fights the steel. It takes the shape the cut gives it and keeps growing around the wound, and that is how a forest turns a knife into a craft.
variants.original: The hard prevails over the soft, the classics say, and so metal governs wood. The axe meets the trunk, the knife meets the branch, and the wild green yields shape it could not find alone. The cut is craft rather than ruin: forest becomes timber, bramble becomes orchard, under an edge that knows what to spare.

variants.candidate: Metal feeds water, the old texts say: dew beads on the cold blade at dawn, drawn out of the air by the chill of the steel. The edge does not pour. It makes the water by being what it is, hard and cold and exact, and the drops gather on the clean line without any effort of its own. What the blade cannot say, the dew says for it, running off into the ground.
variants.original: In the old reckoning water is metal's child: cold iron beads the morning dew, and metal, melted, runs bright as any river. The hard thing does not stay hard. At its finest edge it turns liquid, and what was fixed begins to flow, the clear stream carrying the mountain's sharpness out into the world.

variants.candidate: Fire tames metal, the old texts say, and the forge softens the blade. Cold steel is hard and brittle, and only heat lets it take a shape it can keep. The smith holds the edge in the coals until it glows, works it while it is soft and cools it again. The fire gives the metal nothing it did not already have. It only decides what the metal is made into.
variants.original: The refined prevails over the stubborn: fire alone commands metal. In the forge the unbending learns to bend, ore gives up its rock, and the blade takes whatever shape the flame decides. Heat is the one argument metal cannot win, and what survives the fire comes out finer than what went in.

variants.candidate: Metal answers metal, the old texts say: strike one blade and the one beside it rings at the same pitch. Steel is sharpened on steel, two edges ground together taking a finer line than either could reach alone. Nothing yields in that meeting. Iron piled on iron grows heavier, and an edge with no softer thing to meet has nothing left to cut except its own kind.
variants.original: Like answers like, the classics say: the same note struck twice rings once, and louder. When metal stands beside metal there is no reaction, only reinforcement, ore of one seam, edges off one forge. Such sameness is strength and its own hazard. Two blades in one sheath keep each other keen, or wear each other blunt.
